title: Blocked, not broken
learning_goal: Distinguish reversible competitive inhibition from enzyme denaturation through a visual reaction cycle.
subject: biology
must_not_claim: All enzyme reactions split one substrate into two products.
Substrate forcibly removes a bound inhibitor.
All inhibition is competitive or reversible.
The animation is an atomistic simulation.

approved_facts.statement: A substrate binds at an enzyme active site. In induced fit, binding involves dynamic conformational changes in both enzyme and substrate.
Enzymes lower activation energy. In a schematic cleavage reaction, one substrate can be converted to two products, which leave the enzyme; other enzyme reactions may join or modify substrates.
An enzyme returns to its original state after a catalytic reaction and can catalyze subsequent reactions; it is not consumed as a reactant.
In classical reversible competitive inhibition, an inhibitor occupies the active site and excludes substrate binding while it is bound, without requiring denaturation.

At a fixed concentration of a reversible competitive inhibitor, increasing substrate concentration can reduce inhibition because substrate and inhibitor compete for binding to free enzyme. A substrate does not need to forcibly displace a bound inhibitor.
High temperature can denature a protein enzyme, changing its structure and impairing its function. This is distinct from reversible occupation of an intact active site.
The molecular shapes, trajectories, relative sizes and timing in this animation are schematic teaching illustrations, not atomistic molecular simulations.
